Summary:

This study proposes visual homogeneity as a novel visual property that enables observers perform to several seemingly disparate visual tasks, such as finding an odd item, deciding if two items are same, or judging if an object is symmetric. In Exp 1, the reaction times on several objects were measured in human subjects. In Exp 2, visual homogeneity of each object was calculated based on the reaction time data. The visual homogeneity scores predicted reaction times. This value was also correlated with the BOLD signals in a specific region anterior to LO. Similar methods were used to analyze reaction time and fMRI data in a symmetry detection task. It is concluded that visual homogeneity is an important feature that enables observers to solve these two tasks.

Strengths:

(1) The writing is very clear. The presentation of the study is informative.

(2) This study includes several behavioral and fMRI experiments. I appreciate the scientific rigor of the authors.

Weaknesses:

Before addressing the manuscript itself, I would like to comment the review process first. Having read the lasted revised manuscript, I shared many of the concerns raised by the two reviewers in the last two rounds of review. It appears that the authors have disagreed with the majority of comments made by the two reviewers. If so, I strongly recommend that the authors proceed to make this revision as a Version of Record and conclude this review process. According to eLife's policy that the authors have the right to make a Version of Record at any time during the review process, and I fully respect that right. However, I also ask that the authors respect the reviewer's right to retain the comments regarding this paper.

Beside that, I still have several further questions about this study.

(1) My main concern with this paper is the way visual homogeneity is computed. On page 10, lines 188-192, it says: "we then asked if there is any point in this multidimensional representation such that distances from this point to the target-present and target-absent response vectors can accurately predict the target-present and target-absent response times with a positive and negative correlation respectively (see Methods)". This is also true for the symmetry detection task. If I understand correctly, the reference point in this perceptual space was found by deliberating satisfying the negative and positive correlations in response times. And then on page 10, lines 200-205, it shows that the positive and negative correlations actually exist. This logic is confusing. The positive and negative correlations emerge only because this method is optimized to do so. It seems more reasonable to identify the reference point of this perceptual space independently, without using the reaction time data. Otherwise, the inference process sounds circular. A simple way is to just use the mean point of all objects in Exp 1, without any optimization towards reaction time data.

I raised this question in my initial review. However, the authors did not address whether the positive and negative correlations still hold if the mean point is defined as the reference point without any optimization. The authors also argue that it is similar to a case of fitting a straight line. It is fine that the authors insist on the straight line (e.g., correlation). However, I would not call "straight line correlations" a "quantitative model" as a high-profile journals like eLife. Please remove all related arguments of a novel quantitative model.

(2) Visual homogeneity (at least given the current form) is an unnecessary term. It is similar to distractor heterogeneity/distractor variability/distractor saliency in literature. However, the authors attempt to claim it as a novel concept. Both R1 and me raised this question in the very first review. However, the authors refused to revise the manuscript. In the last review, I mentioned this and provided some example sentences claiming novelty. The authors only revised the last sentence of the abstract, and even did not bother to revise the last sentence of significance: "we show that these tasks can be solved using a simple property WE DEFINE as visual homogeneity". Also, lines 851 still shows "we have defined a NOVEL image property, visual homogeneity...". I am confused about whether the authors agree or disagree that "visual homogeneity is an unnecessary term". If the authors agree, they should completely remove the related phrase throughout the paper. If not, they should keep all these and state the reasons. I don't think this is a correct approach to revising a manuscript.

(3) If the authors agree that visual homogeneity is not new, I suggest a complete rewrite of the title, abstract, significance, and introduction. Let me ask a simple question, can we remove "visual homogeneity" and use some more well-established term like "image feature similarity"? If yes, visual homogeneity is unnecessary.

(4) If I understand it correctly, one of the key findings of this paper is "the response times for target-present searches were positively correlated with visual homogeneity. By contrast, the response times for target-absent searches were negatively correlated with visual homogeneity" (lines 204-207). I think the authors have already acknowledged that this positive correlation is not surprising at all because it reflects the classic target-distractor similarity effect. If this is the case, please completely remove the positive correlation as a novel prediction and finding.

(5) In my last review, I mentioned the seminal paper by Duncan and Humphreys (1989) has clearly stated that "difficulty increases with increased similarity of targets to nontargets and decreased similarity between nontargets" (the sentence in their abstract). Here, "similarity between nontargets" is the same as the visual homogeneity defined here. Similar effects have been shown in Duncan (1989) and Nagy, Neriani, and Young (2005). See also the inconsistent results in Nagy& Thomas, 2003, Vicent, Baddeley, Troscianko&Gilchrist, 2009. More recently, Wei Ji Ma has systematically investigated the effects of heterogeneous distractors in visual search. I think the introduction part of Wei Ji Ma's paper (2020) provides a nice summary of this line of research.

Thanks to the authors' revision, I now better understand the negative correlation. The between-distrator similarity mentioned above describes the heterogeneity of distractors WITHIN an image. However, if I understand it correctly, this study aims to address the negative correlation of reaction time and target-absent stimuli ACROSS images. In other words, why do humans show a shorter reaction time to an image of four pigeons than to an image of four dogs (as shown in Figure 2C), simply because the later image is closer to the reference point of the image space. In this sense, this negative correlation is indeed not the same as distractor heterogeneity. However, this is known as the saliency effect or oddball effects. For example, it seems quite natural to me that humans respond faster to a fish image if the image set contains many images of four-leg dogs that look very different from fish. If this is indeed a saliency effect, why should we define a new term "visual homogeneity"?

(6) The section "key predictions" is quite straightforward. I understand the logic of positive and negative correlations. However, what is the physical meaning of "decision boundary" (Fig. 1G) here? How does the "decision boundary" map on the image space?

(7) In my opinion, one of the advantages of this study is the fMRI dataset, which is valuable because previous studies did not collect fMRI data. The key contribution may be the novel brain region associated with display heterogeneity. If this is the case, I would suggest using a more parametric way to measure this region. For example, one can use Gabor stimuli and systematically manipulate the variations of multiple Gabor stimuli, the same logic also applies to motion direction. If this study uses static Gabor, random dot motion, object images that span from low-level to high-level visual stimuli, and consistently shows that the stimulus heterogeneity is encoded in one brain region, I would say this finding is valuable. But this sounds another experiment. In other words, it is insufficient to claim a new brain region given the current form of the manuscript.

Reviewers:
- Anonymous Reviewer

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.93033.4.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.93033.4.sa3)

Summary of the review process from the Reviewing Editor:

The authors and the reviewers did not agree on several important points made in this paper. The reviewers were critical of the operationalisation of the concept of visual homogeneity (VH), and questioned its validity. For instance, they found it unsatisfying that VH was not calculated on the basis of images themselves, but on the basis of reaction times instead. The authors responded by providing further explanation and argumentation for the importance of this novel concept, but the reviewers were not persuaded. The reviewers also pointed out some data features that did not fit the theory (e.g., overlapping VH between present and absent stimuli), which the authors acknowledge as a point that needs further refining. Finally, the reviewers pointed out that the new so-called visual homogeneity brain region does not overlap very much in the two studies, to which the authors have responded that it is remarkable that there is even partial overlap, given the many confounding differences between the two studies. Altogether, the authors have greatly elaborated their case for VH as an important concept, but the reviewers were not persuaded, and we conclude that the current evidence does not yet meet the high bar for declaring that a novel image property, visual homogeneity, is computed in a localised brain region.

results.result: Experiment 1 measured perceptual dissimilarities between 32 natural objects using an oddball detection task, yielding highly accurate (98.8±0.9%) and consistent (r=0.91, p<0.0001) responses across 16 participants. The reciprocal of response time was used as a measure of perceptual distance, and multidimensional scaling was applied to reconstruct the underlying perceptual space.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 describe a well-established behavioral paradigm with appropriate sample size (n=16), high accuracy, and strong inter-subject reliability. The use of reciprocal RT as perceptual distance is supported by citation (C26), and the MDS approach for reconstructing perceptual space is standard and validated by prior work (C27).

results.result: In Experiment 2, 16 participants performed a target present/absent search task during fMRI. Visual homogeneity (distance from an optimized center in perceptual space) was significantly smaller for target-present than target-absent arrays. Response times for target-present searches were positively correlated with visual homogeneity (r=0.68, p<0.0001), while target-absent searches showed a negative correlation (r=−0.71, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 report the core behavioral finding with appropriate statistics, significant p-values, and opposite correlations as predicted. The model has only 5 free parameters (C163) and was validated through multiple control analyses (C37-C39). The opposite correlations for present/absent conditions are theoretically motivated and empirically robust.

results.result: The range of visual homogeneity values for target-present and target-absent searches overlap, suggesting that visual homogeneity contributes to but does not fully determine task performance. The authors propose that visual homogeneity provides an initial first guess that can be refined through detailed scrutiny.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 acknowledge an important limitation: the model does not fully explain all variance. This is a reasonable interpretation given the observed overlap in VH values and is consistent with the authors' framing of VH as contributing to the initial phase of target selection (C90).

results.result: Multiple validation analyses confirmed the robustness of the visual homogeneity model: (1) deep neural network representations yielded similar predictions (C37), (2) optimization converged to the same center across random initializations (C38), (3) leave-one-out cross-validation yielded similar correlations (r=0.63 for present, r=−0.63 for absent; C39), (4) average distance to other objects predicted VH (C40), and (5) equal weighting of target and distractor was optimal in LO (C41).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 describe rigorous validation analyses that address potential concerns about circularity, overfitting, and model assumptions. The cross-validation (C39) and convergence tests (C38) are appropriate, and the use of DNNs (C37) provides independent support for the approach.

results.result: Visual homogeneity can explain oddball target present/absent judgements during visual search.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is a summary conclusion supported by the combined evidence from C32-C34 (behavioral correlations), C37-C41 (validation analyses), and the theoretical framework (C9-C14). The conclusion is appropriately qualified by acknowledging that VH does not explain all variance (C35, C90).

results.result: Same/different responses can be predicted using visual homogeneity, with 'same' responses correlated with target-absent judgements and 'different' responses correlated with target-present judgements.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 reports results from Appendix 4, which is not provided in the main text. Without access to the appendix, we cannot evaluate sample size, statistical tests, effect sizes, or potential confounds. The claim is plausible given the theoretical framework but requires verification.

results.result: Visual homogeneity is an image-computable property that remains stable across tasks and experimental contexts, and can be empirically estimated as the reciprocal of target-absent response times in visual search.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 make strong assertions about the stability and generalizability of VH across contexts, but the supporting evidence is in Appendix 5 (not provided). While the theoretical motivation is clear, empirical validation of context-independence requires careful experimental manipulation and is critical to the claim that VH is an intrinsic image property (C100, C128).

results.result: fMRI analysis revealed that visual homogeneity is encoded in a localized region (VH) just anterior to the lateral occipital cortex. Mean activations in VH were strongly correlated with visual homogeneity but uncorrelated with response times overall. By contrast, EVC and LO showed negative correlations with RT, while parietal and prefrontal regions showed positive correlations with RT.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 report the key neuroimaging finding with appropriate searchlight analysis, cross-validation across participant groups (C49), and dissociation from RT-related activations (C50-C52). The localization is anatomically specific and the pattern of correlations is consistent with the theoretical predictions (C20-C21).

results.result: Neural dissimilarities in the lateral occipital (LO) region best matched perceptual dissimilarities measured in visual search, consistent with previous studies. This suggests that neural representations in LO correspond to the perceptual space on which visual homogeneity computations are performed.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 report a standard representational similarity analysis with results consistent with prior literature (multiple citations in C55). The finding that LO encodes perceptual dissimilarities provides the foundation for the VH computation and is well-supported by both current data and previous work.

results.result: Neural responses to target-present displays can be predicted as a linear sum of target and distractor responses with roughly equal weights.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 reports results from Appendix 6 (not provided). This is an important validation of the averaging assumption (C9-C11) underlying the VH model, but without access to the appendix, we cannot evaluate the quality of the fits, statistical tests, or whether equal weighting was significantly better than alternatives.

results.result: Experiment 3 measured perceptual dissimilarities for 64 baton shapes (32 symmetric, 32 asymmetric) using oddball detection. Participants (n=15) were highly accurate (98.5±1.33%) and consistent (r=0.88, p<0.0001). Multidimensional scaling revealed that symmetric objects are generally more spread apart than asymmetric objects in perceptual space.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 describe a well-designed experiment with appropriate sample size, high accuracy, and strong reliability. The observation that symmetric objects are more spread apart (C60) is a key prediction of the VH framework and is supported by the MDS visualization (Figure 5B).

results.result: In Experiment 4, 14 participants performed a symmetry detection task during fMRI. Visual homogeneity was significantly larger for symmetric than asymmetric objects (p<0.05). For asymmetric objects, response times were positively correlated with VH (r=0.56, p<0.001), while for symmetric objects, response times were negatively correlated with VH (r=−0.39, p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 report the symmetry detection results with appropriate statistics and opposite correlations as predicted. The correlations are somewhat weaker than in Experiment 2 (C33-C34), but still significant and in the predicted directions. The lower correlation for symmetric objects (r=−0.39) may reflect greater task difficulty or individual differences.

results.result: The range of visual homogeneity values for asymmetric and symmetric objects overlap, suggesting that VH contributes to but does not fully determine symmetry detection. Leave-one-out cross-validation yielded similar correlations (r=0.44 for asymmetric, r=−0.39 for symmetric, p<0.05 in both cases).
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 appropriately acknowledge the limitations of the VH model for symmetry detection and provide cross-validation evidence. The overlap in VH values (C66) and the interpretation that VH provides an initial guess (C67) are consistent with the authors' framing for visual search (C35-C36).

results.result: Visual homogeneity can predict symmetry perception, and the same computation (distance from a center in perceptual space) explains two disparate property-based visual tasks: symmetry perception and visual search.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are summary conclusions supported by the combined evidence from Experiments 1-4. The finding that a single computational principle (distance-to-center) explains both tasks is novel and well-supported by the behavioral and neuroimaging data, though the model does not explain all variance in either task.

results.result: During symmetry detection, visual homogeneity is encoded in a localized VH region that overlaps with the VH region identified during visual search. Mean activations in VH were poorly correlated with response times overall, while parietal and prefrontal regions showed strong correlations with RT, consistent with their role in attentional modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 report the key neuroimaging finding for symmetry detection with appropriate searchlight analysis and dissociation from RT-related activations. The overlap with the VH region from Experiment 2 (C72) is reported with reference to Appendix 8, and the pattern of correlations is consistent with theoretical predictions.

results.result: During symmetry detection, neural dissimilarities in LO best matched perceptual dissimilarities from visual search, while mean activations in VH best matched visual homogeneity. This suggests that visual homogeneity is encoded by the VH region using object representations from the adjoining LO region.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 report representational similarity analyses that are consistent with the findings from Experiment 2 (C53-C55) and support the proposed computational architecture. The finding that LO encodes perceptual space while VH encodes distance-to-center is theoretically motivated and empirically supported.

results.result: Target-absent response times predict symmetry detection with opposite correlations for asymmetric (positive) and symmetric (negative) objects. This reconfirms that a common decision variable, visual homogeneity, drives both target present/absent and symmetry judgements.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 report results from Appendix 9 (not provided). This is an important cross-task validation showing that VH estimated from one task (visual search) predicts performance in another (symmetry detection), but without access to the appendix, we cannot evaluate the strength of the evidence.

results.result: By adjusting the center of perceptual space, visual homogeneity can predict categorization responses for animals, dogs, and Labradors. The default VH (reciprocal of target-absent search time) also predicts categorization responses, suggesting that VH computations can serve as a decision variable for object categorization.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 report reanalysis of prior data (Mohan and Arun, 2012) showing that VH can explain categorization. This is an interesting extension, but the evidence is in Appendix 10 (not provided). The claim that default VH predicts categorization (C82) is particularly strong and requires careful evaluation of whether the category centers are indeed close to the default center.

results.result: A single decision variable (visual homogeneity) can be used to solve three disparate visual tasks (visual search, same/different, and symmetry detection). Visual homogeneity is the underlying decision variable at least for oddball visual search tasks and could be an additional driving factor for making decisions during visual search more generally.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are the main conclusions of the study, supported by the combined evidence from Experiments 1-4 and the additional analyses. The claim is appropriately qualified (C85: 'at least for oddball visual search'; C86: 'could be an additional driving factor'), acknowledging that VH does not explain all variance and may not apply to all forms of visual search.

results.result: Visual homogeneity resolves the puzzle of systematic variation in target-absent search times, which cannot be explained by target-distractor dissimilarity alone. It also explains why we sometimes know a target is present without knowing its exact location, because VH arises in high-level visual areas with coarse spatial information. However, VH does not completely explain all variance in oddball search times.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 provide important context and interpretation of the findings. The observation that target-absent slopes are typically twice target-present slopes (C87) is well-established (Wolfe, 1998), and the explanation via VH (C88) is novel and supported by the data. The acknowledgment of limitations (C90) is appropriate.

results.result: Visual homogeneity resolves the puzzle in same-different tasks that 'same' responses are faster than 'different' responses, contrary to the prediction that zero difference should be slowest. VH provides a simple decision rule and explains why some images elicit faster 'same' responses than others.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 provide an interesting interpretation of how VH resolves a known puzzle in same-different tasks. However, the empirical support is in Appendix 4 (not provided), and the interpretation assumes that VH is the primary driver of same-different responses, which may be an oversimplification.

results.result: Visual homogeneity indicates an indirect mechanism for symmetry detection that does not invoke special symmetry computations. Symmetric objects have high VH because they have repeated parts, while asymmetric objects have low VH because they have disparate parts.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 contrast the VH account with traditional symmetry detection models (C94, supported by citations) and provide a mechanistic explanation for why symmetric objects have higher VH (C96-C97, supported by citation to Pramod and Arun, 2018). The indirect mechanism is supported by the data from Experiments 3-4.

results.result: Visual homogeneity is correlated with the average distance to other objects (as in Pramod and Arun, 2018), but VH is an intrinsic image property that is independent of experimental context, whereas average distance depends on the set of objects used for averaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 make an important conceptual distinction between VH and average distance. The correlation between VH and average distance (C99) is reported in Appendix 1, and the context-independence of VH (C101) is reported in Appendix 4. Without access to these appendices, we cannot fully evaluate whether VH is truly context-independent or whether the distinction from average distance is empirically justified.

results.result: Visual homogeneity is encoded in a specific brain region (VH) located just anterior to the lateral occipital (LO) region in both visual search and symmetry detection tasks. This finding is consistent with norm-based encoding in IT neurons and face recognition. The proximity of VH to LO suggests that VH computations are based on object representations in LO.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 summarize the key neuroimaging findings with appropriate citations to prior work on norm-based encoding (C108). The localization of VH anterior to LO is consistent across tasks (C107, C109), and the speculation that VH computations are based on LO representations (C110) is reasonable given the proximity and the RSA results (C77).

results.result: The VH region overlaps with the recently reported ventral stream attention module. Previous studies found larger activations for animate vs. inanimate objects in this region, which can be explained by the current finding that animate objects have smaller VH and thus weaker VH region activation. Visual homogeneity may be an additional organizing factor in human ventral temporal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 relate the current findings to prior literature with appropriate citations (C117, C118). The explanation of animate/inanimate differences via VH (C119-C120) is supported by the data (p<0.05) and provides a novel interpretation of previous findings. The suggestion that VH is an organizing factor (C121) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: Previous studies reported larger activations for symmetric vs. asymmetric objects in the vicinity of VH. This can be explained by the current finding that symmetric objects have larger visual homogeneity, leading to greater VH region activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 relate the current findings to prior literature (Sasaki et al., 2005; Van Meel et al., 2019) and provide a mechanistic explanation. The explanation is supported by the data from Experiment 4 (C63, C76) and is consistent with the VH framework.

results.result: Visual homogeneity is defined as the distance of a visual image to a central point in the underlying perceptual representation. It can be reliably estimated as the inverse of target-absent response time in visual search and appears to be an intrinsic image property unaffected by experimental context.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 provide the operational definition of VH. The definition (C126) is clear, and the estimation method (C127) is supported by the data from Experiments 1-2. However, the claim that VH is context-independent (C128) relies on Appendix 4 (not provided), which is critical for establishing VH as an intrinsic image property.

results.result: Many property-based visual tasks can be solved using visual homogeneity as a decision variable, localized to a specific region anterior to the lateral occipital cortex. This represents an important first step in demonstrating a quantitative, falsifiable model and localized neural substrate for property-based visual tasks. Visual homogeneity computations might contribute to a variety of other visual tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 are the main conclusions of the study, appropriately qualified as a 'first step' (C133) and with speculation about future applications (C134). The conclusions are supported by the combined evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging experiments across multiple tasks.

results.result: The visual homogeneity model has only 5 free parameters (the coordinates of the center in perceptual space). The optimum center remained stable across random initializations. The number of dimensions (5) was selected based on analysis showing that correlations with RT increased from 1-5 dimensions, plateaued from 5-9, and decreased beyond 9.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C166 describe the model specification and validation. The model is parsimonious (5 parameters for predicting both present and absent RTs), the optimization is stable (C164), and the dimensionality selection is data-driven (C165-C166). This is appropriate methodological rigor.

results.result: The authors claim that visual homogeneity (VH) is a novel concept that unifies three disparate property-based visual tasks (visual search, same/different, and symmetry detection) under a single decision variable, defined as the distance of a visual image to a central point in perceptual representation space.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly challenged the novelty claim, stating that VH is 'similar to distractor heterogeneity/distractor variability/distractor saliency in literature' and that the authors 'attempt to claim it as a novel concept' without justification. One reviewer noted 'visual homogeneity (at least given the current form) is an unnecessary term' and questioned whether the authors could 'remove "visual homogeneity" and use some more well-established term like "image feature similarity"'. The editor summarized that 'the evidence provided for the very strong claims of homogeneity as a novel concept in vision science, separable from existing concepts such as target saliency, is incomplete.'

results.result: The authors report opposite correlations between visual homogeneity and response times: positive correlations for target-present searches (r=0.68) and asymmetric objects (r=0.56), and negative correlations for target-absent searches (r=-0.71) and symmetric objects (r=-0.39).
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised fundamental concerns about the circularity and interpretation of these correlations. One reviewer stated 'the positive and negative correlations emerge only because this method is optimized to do so' through center-fitting. Another noted that 'the positive correlation is not surprising at all because it reflects the classic target-distractor similarity effect' and should not be presented as novel. The reviewing editor noted that 'the reviewers were critical of the operationalisation of the concept of visual homogeneity (VH), and questioned its validity' particularly regarding how VH was calculated from reaction times rather than image properties directly.

results.result: The authors claim to have identified a novel brain region (area VH) anterior to lateral occipital cortex that encodes visual homogeneity in both visual search and symmetry detection tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers fundamentally rejected this claim due to poor overlap between VH regions across experiments. One reviewer stated 'VHsymmetry and VHdetection are nearly non-overlapping. This is a fundamental problem with the claim of discovering a new area.' The authors acknowledged confounding differences (stimuli, visual field, participants) but reviewers responded that 'it is up to the authors to show that their definition of a new "area VH" is convincing when the confounding differences are resolved' and that 'declaring a new brain area depends on much more work than is done here.' The editor concluded 'the current evidence does not yet meet the high bar for declaring that a novel image property, visual homogeneity, is computed in a localised brain region.'

results.result: The authors acknowledge that visual homogeneity values overlap between conditions (target-present/absent, symmetric/asymmetric) and that VH contributes but does not fully determine task performance, proposing it provides an initial first guess that can be refined through detailed scrutiny.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted this overlap as problematic for the theory. One reviewer stated 'the reviewers also pointed out some data features that did not fit the theory (e.g., overlapping VH between present and absent stimuli), which the authors acknowledge as a point that needs further refining.' Another reviewer commented that 'the authors' acknowledgement of flaws in the ms does not argue in favor of publication, but rather just the opposite.' The authors' interpretation that VH provides a 'first guess' was not directly addressed by reviewers but the overall model limitations were emphasized.

results.result: The authors performed validation analyses showing that: (1) deep neural network representations can predict target present/absent responses via distance-to-center computations, (2) the optimization procedure yields stable centers across random initializations, and (3) leave-one-out cross-validation yields similar correlations (r=0.63 for target-present, r=-0.63 for target-absent).
results.evaluation: Reviewers dismissed these validation efforts as insufficient to address fundamental concerns. One reviewer stated 'none of the results described above answer the concern about how center-fitting undercuts the evidentiary value of their main results' and that 'the point of the original comment was that center-fitting should not be done in the first place because it introduces unknowable effects.' Another noted that using deep networks 'cannot provide stronger evidence that compensates for what was lacking in the human data' and that 'the authors can experiment on side questions for as long as they please' but these do not address core methodological problems.

results.result: Participants showed high accuracy (95-98.8%) and consistent response times across participants (r=0.47-0.91) in all four experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the basic behavioral data quality. The editor noted 'this study uses carefully designed experiments to generate a useful behavioural and neuroimaging dataset on visual cognition' and one reviewer acknowledged 'the writing is very clear' and 'I appreciate the scientific rigor of the authors.' The behavioral consistency was not questioned.

results.result: Neural representations in lateral occipital (LO) cortex match with perceptual dissimilarities measured from visual search, with the best correlation occurring in LO compared to other visual regions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this finding. The editor stated 'the results provide solid evidence for the involvement of higher-order visual cortex in processing visual oddballs and asymmetry.' This aspect of the neural data showing LO's role in perceptual representation was consistent with prior literature and not disputed.

results.result: The authors report that same/different responses correlate with target-absent/present judgments, and that target-absent response times predict symmetry detection with opposite correlations for symmetric versus asymmetric objects, supporting a common decision variable (visual homogeneity) across tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers rejected the interpretation of a common mechanism. One stated 'there is only a "challenge" if you accept the authors' a priori assumption that all of these tasks must have a common explanation and rely on a single neural mechanism. I do not accept that assumption.' Another noted 'there is still no reason to think that same-different judgments are based on a mythical boundary halfway between the two' and that 'same/different will have a boundary very close to the "same" end of the continuum' rather than at a midpoint as the model assumes.

results.result: Mean activations in the VH region are uncorrelated with response times overall, while activations in early visual cortex (EVC) and LO are negatively correlated with response times, and parietal/prefrontal regions are strongly correlated with response times consistent with attentional modulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not specifically challenge these dissociations between VH activity and response times versus other regions. This pattern was presented as supporting evidence that VH encodes something distinct from task difficulty, though the overall VH concept was rejected on other grounds.

results.result: The authors claim visual homogeneity is an intrinsic image property that remains stable across experimental contexts and can be empirically estimated as the reciprocal of target-absent response times.
results.evaluation: Reviewers challenged the claim of VH as an intrinsic image property. One stated 'they found it unsatisfying that VH was not calculated on the basis of images themselves, but on the basis of reaction times instead.' Another noted 'if stimulus complexity is what matters, as the authors agree here, then it is incumbent on them to measure stimulus complexity' rather than deriving it from behavior. The claim of context-independence was not directly evaluated but the overall operationalization was rejected.

comparisons.comparison: Both address the main novelty claim (C84, C126, C132). OpenEval finds the conclusions SUPPORTED and appropriately qualified, while peer reviewers strongly challenge novelty, stating VH is 'similar to distractor heterogeneity' and 'an unnecessary term'. Major disagreement on whether VH represents a genuinely novel concept.

Both evaluate the core behavioral correlations (C33, C34, C64, C65). OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED with appropriate statistics and theoretical motivation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising fundamental concerns about circularity from center-fitting and noting the positive correlation 'reflects the classic target-distractor similarity effect' rather than novelty.

Both address VH neural localization claims (C47, C48, C71, C72, C107, C109). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate searchlight analysis and cross-validation. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED due to poor overlap between VH regions across experiments, stating 'VHsymmetry and VHdetection are nearly non-overlapping' and rejecting the claim of discovering a new area.

Both discuss model limitations and overlap in VH values (C35, C36, C66, C67, C90). OpenEval finds the acknowledgment of limitations SUPPORTED and reasonable. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting the overlap as problematic for the theory and that 'acknowledgement of flaws does not argue in favor of publication.'

Both evaluate validation analyses (C37, C38, C39, C163, C164). OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED as rigorous controls addressing circularity and overfitting. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, dismissing these efforts as insufficient, stating 'center-fitting should not be done in the first place' and that DNN validation 'cannot provide stronger evidence.'

Both address behavioral paradigm quality (C24, C25, C29, C30, C31, C58, C59, C61, C62). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate sample size and reliability. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging 'carefully designed experiments' and 'scientific rigor' without challenging basic data quality.

Both evaluate LO's role in encoding perceptual dissimilarities (C53, C54, C55, C75, C77). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED and consistent with prior literature. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, noting 'solid evidence for the involvement of higher-order visual cortex' and not disputing this aspect.

Both address cross-task generalization claims (C43, C79, C80). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to missing appendix data but finds the claim plausible. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, rejecting the interpretation of a common mechanism and questioning the assumption that 'all of these tasks must have a common explanation.'

Both discuss dissociation between VH activity and RT-related activations (C50, C51, C52, C73, C74). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as evidence VH encodes something distinct from task difficulty. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, not specifically challenging these dissociations.

Both address VH as intrinsic image property and context-independence (C44, C45, C100, C101, C127, C128). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to missing appendix data but notes theoretical motivation. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, challenging that VH was 'calculated on the basis of reaction times instead' of image properties directly.
OpenEval finds the summary conclusion (C42) SUPPORTED by combined behavioral and validation evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this summary claim.
OpenEval rates results from Appendix 4 (C43) as UNCERTAIN due to missing data. Peer reviewers address C43 in R8 regarding cross-task mechanisms but not specifically the appendix validation.
OpenEval rates Appendix 6 results on averaging assumption (C56) as UNCERTAIN due to missing data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval finds Experiment 3 design and symmetry spacing results (C57-C60) SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers address related behavioral data quality in R6 but not these specific claims.

OpenEval finds symmetry detection correlations (C61-C65) SUPPORTED despite being weaker than Experiment 2. Peer reviewers address C64-C65 in R2 regarding circularity concerns but not the full result set.
OpenEval finds acknowledgment of VH limitations for symmetry (C66-C68) SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers address C66-C67 in R4 as problematic but not as a standalone evaluation.
OpenEval finds summary conclusions about unified principle (C69-C70) SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this summary.
OpenEval finds RSA results showing LO encodes perceptual space while VH encodes distance-to-center (C75-C78) SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers address C75, C77 in R7 but not the full architectural claim.
OpenEval rates categorization reanalysis (C81-C83) as UNCERTAIN due to missing Appendix 10. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval finds interpretation of target-absent slopes via VH (C87-C90) SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers address C90 in R4 regarding limitations but not the slope interpretation.
OpenEval rates same-different task interpretation (C91-C93) as UNCERTAIN due to missing appendix. Peer reviewers address related claims in R8 but not these specific claims.
OpenEval finds contrast with traditional symmetry models (C94-C97) SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval rates distinction between VH and average distance (C98-C101) as UNCERTAIN due to missing appendices. Peer reviewers address C100-C101 in R10 but not the full distinction claim.
OpenEval finds neuroimaging summary and norm-based encoding discussion (C107-C110) SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers address C107, C109 in R3 regarding localization but not the norm-based interpretation.
OpenEval finds animate/inanimate differences explanation via VH (C117-C121) SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval finds explanation of prior literature findings (C122-C123) SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval rates operational definition of VH (C126-C128) as UNCERTAIN due to missing appendix on context-independence. Peer reviewers address C126, C128 in R1 and R10 but not as operational definition evaluation.
OpenEval finds main conclusions (C132-C134) SUPPORTED and appropriately qualified. Peer reviewers address C132 in R1 regarding novelty but not the full conclusion set.
OpenEval finds model specification and validation (C163-C166) SUPPORTED with appropriate rigor. Peer reviewers address C163-C164 in R5 regarding validation but not model parsimony.
